title: Rites of Passage
author: Patrick B. Whalen
summary: Patrick Whalen traces his own coming-of-age across three summers—working at a sawmill and playing Irish bars in New York, busking in Seattle with a band, and then enduring Marine Corps boot camp in Southern California—as a meditation on what genuine rites of passage actually require of young men. Drawing on his experience as a Marine veteran and educator, Whalen argues that the most formative element of boot camp is not physical suffering, which most people can endure, but sustained and deliberate humiliation that strips away individualism and forces the recruit to negotiate between fear, resentment, self-disgust, and prudent self-management. The piece suggests that modern culture has largely eliminated the conditions under which this kind of formation occurs naturally, and that something essential is lost when young men move from adolescence to adulthood without encountering genuinely demanding institutional demands on their character.
points: Whalen narrates three summers of increasingly demanding formation—laborer, street musician, Marine recruit—as a personal map of how young men are shaped by difficulty and context.
Physical suffering in boot camp is described as manageable; the deeper and more lasting formation comes from sustained, systematic humiliation designed to dissolve the self and rebuild it.

Rituals like being addressed only by rank, losing one's first name, and writing accountability letters to imagined military widows serve to create a new collective identity in place of the individual one.
The piece frames rites of passage not as ceremonial events but as extended processes that require genuine stakes, real consequences, and demands the initiate cannot fully control.
Implicit throughout is a critique of contemporary education and childhood as structures that protect young men from the very experiences that would form them.
quotes: I traded my guitar for a gun and spent months crawling in the dirt in Southern California alongside hundreds of other young men who were intent on becoming United States Marines.
The pain in bootcamp is mundane. If you're in decent shape, it's not a problem. What is much more thorough and impactful, however, is the sustained humiliation.
Humiliation is like a good marinade before searing the meat. It makes it pliable for the work to come.

You have no first name and if you find yourself having to communicate with a drill instructor, you must only use the third person to refer to yourself. There is no 'self' now...just another Marine recruit among many.

Any infraction is rewarded with physical pain and degradation, and sometimes an added psychological element if you do something stupid: you might have to write letters to your fellow recruits' mothers, wives, and children to explain why your selfishness, incompetence, weakness, or stupidity has caused their son, husband, or father to die unnecessarily.

To succeed in this environment requires negotiating a sustainable truce between your fear of pain and humiliation, your resentment at being forced into those feelings, your own disgust with yourself for feeling them in the first place, and a prudent management of your physical capacity for suffering.
